A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Excited Pfaffians and Multi-State Importance Sampling work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original VMC calculations for second-row atoms, 12 molecules, carbon-dimer and ethylene potential energy surfaces, and 33 beryllium states, together with runtime measurements and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds effective-sample-size measurements, an architecture comparison, expanded runtime measurements and a compute-budget-matched NES experiment.

M1.justification: The architecture, sample-pooling strategy and spin snapping remain. However, the written computational specification changes: Eq. 7 uses squared overlap, the normalizer and bridge-system expressions are revised, and the pretraining Procrustes rotations are corrected. These are limited formula-level corrections; the PDFs do not establish an implementation change or rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same Li–Ne atoms, 12 molecules, 33-state beryllium calculation, carbon-dimer dissociation and crossing geometries, and ethylene torsion and pyramidalization. The added analyses reuse this coverage; their different model configurations and compute budgets do not introduce new tasks or populations.

E2.justification: Appendix I newly evaluates the naive architecture with separate orbitals per state against Excited Pfaffians; v1 only discussed its memory requirements. Appendix N also includes Szabo et al. (2024) in the expanded runtime comparisons, whereas v1 Appendix L's compute estimates focused on NES. Existing accuracy comparators remain.

E3.justification: Appendix N replaces assumption-based compute estimates with A100 timing protocols: Adam/KFAC measurements at 1,000 walkers are scaled to 4,000, while SPRING is measured at 4,000. It adds a 12-state NES comparison with approximately 4,500 steps per geometry under the proposed method's compute budget. Appendix I introduces a single-determinant architecture control. The reported VMC learning-rate schedule also changes from 0.02/(1+1/10000) to 0.02/(1+t/10000), without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix E tests whether MSIS sample pooling remains effective across systems and electron/atom counts. Appendix I tests the efficiency and convergence consequences of sharing orbitals, and Appendix N.1 examines NES accuracy under a matched compute budget. These substantially extend the retained MSIS-removal ablation and state-crossing analyses.

E5.justification: New Figure 11 reports effective-sample-size averages over states with standard-deviation error bars. These describe variation across states, not repeated training runs. Existing parenthesized energy uncertainties remain unchanged, and neither version documents an increased seed or repeated-run count.

E6.justification: The original energy values in v1 Tables 4–8 are retained in v2 Tables 9–13. Substantial new results include normalized effective sample sizes, architecture convergence and optimizer-dependent timings: Table 5 reports cumulative C2 speedups of 208 times with Adam and 46 times with KFAC versus SPRING. New Table 6 reports a first excitation of 1.3817 eV for budget-limited NES versus 0.4294 eV for the proposed method. These are added comparisons, not improvements to the retained energy results.

T1.justification: Appendix D corrects the joint-variance expression in Eq. 43 by removing extraneous state-count factors and revising the intermediate equality. It also removes v1's assertion that estimating normalization ratios changes the bound only by O(1/Nb). Equation 9 now explicitly concerns overlap magnitude. These repair or narrow the existing mathematical treatment without introducing a new theoretical framework.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and discussion retain the same central contributions: MSIS variance reduction, efficient shared-orbital Excited Pfaffians, generalization across structures and compounds, and many-state calculations. The principal novelty and headline carbon-dimer and beryllium claims remain; new experiments mainly provide additional support.

C2.justification: The ethylene state-swap explanation changes from self-reinforcing overlap-penalty ordering in v1 Appendix J to a Rydberg–valence crossing and a parameter-similarity hypothesis in v2 Appendix L. v2 also interprets the C2 swap as an avoided crossing, explicitly excludes transfer to unseen structures, and adds qualifications concerning conical intersections and residual spin-state mixtures.

D1.justification: New Appendix O.2 states that the implementation is publicly available and supplies a code link. The added comparisons disclose hardware, determinant constraints and NES pretraining requirements. Table 12 also corrects the ethylene caption from separate to joint training, consistent with v1's main text and Figure 12; this does not establish a newly joint experiment. Most existing implementation documentation is retained.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly relates MSIS to the balance heuristic through Veach and Guibas (1995) and Owen and Zhou (2000). Additional citations support effective sample size, transfer limitations and state-crossing interpretations, while the Folx reference is removed. These refine selected connections to prior work without substantially changing the overall research positioning.

P1.justification: The six-section main narrative and most prose remain. Changes include localized background and limitations edits, rewritten compute-time and ethylene explanations, inserted appendix sections, and corrected terminology, affiliation/contact text and conference footer. The additional scientific content does not entail wholesale narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial quantitative displays: Figures 11, 12 and 17 show effective sample size, architecture convergence and runtime scaling, while Tables 2–6 present sample counts, timings and budget-limited excitation energies. Original figures are retained and relocated or renumbered; Figure 2's caption is shortened and several table captions are corrected.

improvement.justification: v1's key compute comparisons relied on scaling assumptions. v2 substantially strengthens this central evidence with hardware timings and explicit batch-size scaling, a matched-budget NES experiment, and controlled architecture comparisons. Effective-sample-size diagnostics, mathematical corrections and a code-access statement further improve assessability. A material qualification remains: Table 5 supports 208 times faster C2 steps with Adam but 46 times with KFAC versus SPRING, so the retained headline speedup needs clearer optimizer qualification. Nevertheless, the added evidence substantially improves the paper's support for its efficiency claims.
